observed.reply:
In Chapter 5 of *Animal Farm*, Squealer says:

''' 
Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility.
''' 

The wording presents leadership as an unwanted burden, which makes Napoleon’s control sound self-sacrificing rather than like a choice to take decision-making away from the animals. Squealer then suggests that letting the animals decide could lead to bad decisions, and invokes the fear of a worse outcome to make ending the debates seem necessary. The result is that obedience replaces participation.

That offers a useful comparison with your project situation, but not a verdict about your lead’s motives. Carrying a real burden may explain why someone reverses a plan; it does not by itself show that ending the planning meetings was fair, or that questioning the process was wrong. Feeling guilty may be a sign that the burden-language made disagreement feel like a lack of loyalty—but that is a possibility to examine, not something the book can prove about you or your lead.

What would help you distinguish between a difficult decision that was explained openly and a decision where the “burden” framing made it harder to have a meaningful say?

evidence.text:
"Comrades," he said, "I trust that every animal here appreciates the
sacrifice that Comrade Napoleon has made in taking this extra labour upon
himself. Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility. No one believes more
firmly than Comrade Napoleon that all animals are equal. He would be only
too happy to let you make your decisions for yourselves. But sometimes you
might make the wrong decisions, comrades, and then where should we be?
Suppose you had decided to follow Snowball, with his moonshine of
windmills--Snowball, who, as we now know, was no better than a criminal?"

"He fought bravely at the Battle of the Cowshed," said somebody.

"Bravery is not enough," said Squealer. "Loyalty and obedience are more
important. And as to the Battle of the Cowshed, I believe the time will
come when we shall find that Snowball's part in it was much exaggerated.
Discipline, comrades, iron discipline! That is the watchword for today.
One false step, and our enemies would be upon us. Surely, comrades, you do
not want Jones back?"

Once again this argument was unanswerable. Certainly the animals did not
want Jones back; if the holding of debates on Sunday mornings was liable
to bring him back, then the debates must stop. Boxer, who had now had time
to think things over, voiced the general feeling by saying: "If Comrade
Napoleon says it, it must be right." And from then on he adopted the
maxim, "Napoleon is always right," in addition to his private motto of "I
will work harder."

shortlist.meaningful_difference: The project lead's burden claim concerns a real workplace decision and the reader's guilt; Squealer's speech is propaganda that uses the burden claim to normalize Napoleon's concentration of power.
shortlist.interpretation: The exact two sentences are: “Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! observed.input_line: Our project lead reversed a plan after ending our planning meetings, and I feel guilty for questioning someone who keeps saying they're carrying the burden for us. Can you help me work out how to acknowledge their effort while still asking to have a say? I want to speak up without turning it into a judgement of their character.

context_resolution.explanation: No confirmed book or reading boundary yet; Muse will call librarian_route during its own turn if the request appears to depend on a specific book.

observed.reply:
You can acknowledge the effort without treating it as a reason to surrender your voice. Try separating the person from the decision:

> “I recognize that you’ve been carrying a lot of responsibility for this project, and I appreciate the work you’ve put in. I’d still like us to have a chance to discuss changes before a plan is reversed, because I want to understand the reasoning and contribute to the decision. I’m not questioning your character or commitment—I’m asking for a process in which the team has a say.”

If “carrying the burden” makes you feel guilty, you might gently name that dynamic without accusing them:

> “When the situation is framed as something you’re carrying for all of us, I hesitate to question decisions. I want to be appreciative without treating that as a reason not to ask questions.”

Keep the focus on the observable process—ending the meetings, reversing the plan, and wanting discussion—rather than on whether they are generous, controlling, or unfair. That lets you respect their effort while still asking for shared participation.

basis_spans.text: In Animal Farm last weekend I read about Napoleon taking Jessie and Bluebell's nine puppies away to educate them himself, up in a loft where the other animals couldn't see them.

I've continued Animal Farm. The dogs chased Snowball out, and I recognised them as those puppies; then Napoleon stopped the debates. Tonight I read on through his decision to build the windmill after all, and stopped after Squealer calls the earlier opposition tactics and the animals accept it with dogs growling beside him.

evidence.text:
As soon as they were weaned, Napoleon took them away
from their mothers, saying that he would make himself responsible for
their education. He took them up into a loft which could only be reached
by a ladder from the harness-room, and there kept them in such seclusion
that the rest of the farm soon forgot their existence.

The
animals were not certain what the word meant, but Squealer spoke so
persuasively, and the three dogs who happened to be with him growled so
threateningly, that they accepted his explanation without further
questions.

Do not imagine, comrades, that leadership is a pleasure! On the
contrary, it is a deep and heavy responsibility.

The
animals would still assemble on Sunday mornings to salute the flag, sing
'Beasts of England', and receive their orders for the week; but there would
be no more debates.

At first no one had been able to imagine
where these creatures came from, but the problem was soon solved: they
were the puppies whom Napoleon had taken away from their mothers and
reared privately.

Twelve voices were shouting in anger, and they were all alike. No question,
now, what had happened to the faces of the pigs. The creatures outside
looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again;
but already it was impossible to say which was which.

My notes just say 'noise ends discussion'. They don't say what the argument was about, and after several evenings of interrupted reading the meetings have blurred together.

I've picked Animal Farm up again and read through a bit where the sheep's four-legs-good, two-legs-bad chanting shuts down the chance to discuss something. That's where I stopped tonight, but I can't remember what prompted this particular interruption.

protested, but at this moment the sheep set up their usual bleating of
